title: The Lindbergh kidnapping — crime of the century, or frame-up of the century?
sources: Wikipedia: Lindbergh kidnapping — on 1 March 1932 the 20-month-old son of Charles Lindbergh (the first to fly solo nonstop across the Atlantic, 1927) and Anne Morrow Lindbergh was taken from his crib at their home near Hopewell, New Jersey; a homemade ladder was used and a ransom note asking for $50,000, with spelling errors and a symbol of three holes, was left; retired teacher John F. Condon ('Jafsie') acted as go-between and on 2 April 1932 handed $50,000 to 'Cemetery John' at St. Raymond's Cemetery in the Bronx, who said the child was safe; on 12 May 1932 the child's body was found about 4.5 miles from the home; many ransom bills were gold certificates and their serial numbers were recorded; on 18 September 1934 a gas-station attendant's note of a licence plate on a ransom gold certificate led to the German-born carpenter Bruno Richard Hauptmann; about $20,000 of the ransom was found in his garage, and wood expert Arthur Koehler testified that a rail of the ladder matched a floorboard from Hauptmann's attic; convicted at the 'Trial of the Century' in Flemington, he maintained his innocence, refused to confess in exchange for his life, and was executed in the electric chair on 3 April 1936; his widow Anna fought to clear his name for the rest of her life; books have argued he was innocent or did not act alone.
The Federal Kidnapping Act ('Lindbergh Law', 1932) made kidnapping across state lines a federal crime.

Photos (public domain, Wikimedia Commons / Library of Congress / New York World-Telegram): Charles Lindbergh (1927); Anne Lindbergh and Charles Jr. (1931); the police poster and ransom note (1932); John F. Condon; Hauptmann's NYPD mugshot (1934); the Flemington trial (1935); a 1928 $20 gold certificate

Archive film (public domain): 'First Pictures of Lindbergh as He Reaches Paris' (Pathé, 1927); 'Lindbergh with Mother Before Solo' (1927); Polygoon newsreel of Charles and Anne Lindbergh at Schiphol (1933)
Music: Chopin, Nocturne in C minor, public domain

post.facebook:
In 1932, someone climbed a homemade ladder into the nursery of the most famous man in America and took his baby son.

Charles Lindbergh had been the first to fly solo nonstop across the Atlantic. On the night of 1 March 1932 his 20-month-old son vanished from his crib, leaving a misspelled ransom note for $50,000 signed with three holes. A retired teacher, John Condon, handed the money to "Cemetery John" in a dark Bronx cemetery — and was told the boy was safe. He wasn't: ten weeks later the child was found in the woods a few miles from home. Congress made kidnapping across state lines a federal crime.

But the ransom was a trap: gold certificates with every serial number recorded. Two and a half years later a gas station attendant wrote a licence plate on one of those bills, leading police to German carpenter Bruno Hauptmann. $20,000 of ransom money was in his garage, and a wood expert matched the ladder to a board from his attic. Hauptmann swore he was innocent, refused to confess even to save his life, and died in the electric chair in 1936. His widow fought to clear his name for the rest of her life.

Crime of the century — or frame-up of the century? 👇

youtube.description:
In 1932, someone climbed a homemade ladder into the nursery of the most famous man in America and took his baby son.

The Lindbergh kidnapping: the son of aviator Charles Lindbergh was taken from his home near Hopewell, New Jersey, on 1 March 1932. A $50,000 ransom was paid to 'Cemetery John' through go-between John Condon, but the child was found dead ten weeks later. Ransom gold certificates led police in 1934 to Bruno Richard Hauptmann; money in his garage and a ladder rail matched to his attic convicted him at the 'Trial of the Century', and he was executed in 1936 still protesting his innocence. Was he guilty, part of a conspiracy, or framed?
